title: Loading and transforming in Snowflake
summary: Stages, COPY INTO, Snowpipe and Snowpipe Streaming for loading; streams, tasks, Dynamic Tables and MERGE for transforming; VARIANT for semi-structured data.

blocks.text: Snowflake offers several ingestion paths with different latency and cost profiles, and several ways to transform data incrementally once it lands. This chapter maps each to the patterns from Part IV (batch, micro-batch, streaming, CDC).
27.1 Stages and file formats

A **stage** is a named location of files that Snowflake can read: internal stages live in Snowflake-managed storage (user `@~`, table `@%orders`, or named), external stages point at your bucket through a **storage integration**, which holds a cloud IAM role instead of keys. A **file format** describes how to parse files.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: external stage
blocks.text:
CREATE STORAGE INTEGRATION s3_lake
  TYPE = EXTERNAL_STAGE
  STORAGE_PROVIDER = 'S3'
  ENABLED = TRUE
  STORAGE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake-loader'
  STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS = ('s3://acme-landing/');

CREATE FILE FORMAT ff_parquet TYPE = PARQUET;

CREATE STAGE landing
  URL = 's3://acme-landing/orders/'
  STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_lake
  FILE_FORMAT = ff_parquet;
27.2 Batch loading with COPY INTO

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: COPY INTO
blocks.text:
COPY INTO raw.orders
FROM @landing
PATTERN = '.*2026/11/17/.*[.]parquet'
MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE
ON_ERROR = 'ABORT_STATEMENT';

items: **Load metadata**: Snowflake remembers which files were loaded into each table (for 64 days) and skips them on later COPY runs, so rerunning a load is idempotent by default. `FORCE = TRUE` overrides this and creates duplicates.
**File sizing**: loads parallelize per file. Files of roughly 100-250 MB compressed keep a warehouse busy; thousands of tiny files waste per-file overhead, one 50 GB file uses a single thread.
**Errors**: `ON_ERROR` chooses between aborting, skipping a file or continuing past bad rows; `VALIDATION_MODE` dry-runs a load and returns errors without loading.
**Transform on load**: COPY can select and cast columns from the stage (`COPY INTO t FROM (SELECT $1:id::NUMBER, ... FROM @landing)`), but keep heavy logic in later steps.

blocks.text: 27.3 Continuous loading: Snowpipe and Snowpipe Streaming

head: Path
Unit of ingestion
Typical latency
Compute
Fits
rows: Files, triggered by cloud event notifications
Continuous file arrival in a bucket
Rows sent through an SDK or the Kafka connector

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: auto-ingest pipe
blocks.text:
CREATE PIPE raw.orders_pipe AUTO_INGEST = TRUE AS
  COPY INTO raw.orders
  FROM @landing
  MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE;
-- then point the bucket's event notifications at the pipe's notification channel
-- (SHOW PIPES shows it)

**Snowpipe** is COPY INTO run by Snowflake when a new-file notification arrives (S3 events via SQS, Azure Event Grid, GCS Pub/Sub). It deduplicates by file name with its own load history. **Snowpipe Streaming** skips files entirely: a client opens *channels* into a table and appends rows; each channel tracks an *offset token* the client can read back after a restart to resume exactly where it left off. Pricing models for both have changed over time; check the current documentation.

Snowpipe and file-based COPY both depend on file names for deduplication. A producer that rewrites a file under the same name, or an upstream that re-emits files under new names, breaks exactly-once assumptions. Deduplicate on business keys downstream anyway.
27.4 Streams and tasks

A **stream** is a change-tracking cursor on a table (or view). Querying it returns the rows changed since the stream's offset, with metadata columns `METADATA$ACTION` (INSERT or DELETE), `METADATA$ISUPDATE` and `METADATA$ROW_ID`. An update appears as a DELETE plus an INSERT pair with `ISUPDATE = TRUE`. The offset advances only when the stream is consumed in a DML statement that commits, so a failed run reprocesses the same changes. A **task** runs SQL on a schedule or after another task, on a warehouse or serverless compute.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: stream + task + MERGE
blocks.text:
CREATE STREAM raw.orders_changes ON TABLE raw.orders;

CREATE TASK silver.merge_orders
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  SCHEDULE  = '5 MINUTE'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('raw.orders_changes')
AS
MERGE INTO silver.orders t
USING (
  SELECT * FROM raw.orders_changes
  WHERE METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT'
  QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1
) s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET
  status = s.status, amount = s.amount, updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, status, amount, updated_at)
  VALUES (s.order_id, s.status, s.amount, s.updated_at);

ALTER TASK silver.merge_orders RESUME;

items: The `WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA` condition is evaluated by cloud services, so the warehouse does not start when there is nothing to do.
Deduplicate inside the source subquery: a MERGE where several source rows match one target row is nondeterministic and errors by default.
The `updated_at` guard makes the MERGE safe against out-of-order or replayed changes.
A stream becomes **stale** if not consumed within the table's retention (extended up to a maximum set by `MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS`); it must then be recreated and the target rebuilt.

blocks.text: 27.5 Dynamic Tables

A **Dynamic Table** is declared as a query plus a freshness target. Snowflake works out the dependency graph, schedules refreshes, and refreshes incrementally where the query allows it. It replaces many stream-and-task pipelines with declarative SQL.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: Dynamic Table
blocks.text:
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE gold.daily_revenue
  TARGET_LAG   = '15 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE    = transform_wh
  REFRESH_MODE = AUTO
AS
SELECT TO_DATE(order_ts) AS order_date, region, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM silver.orders
WHERE status <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP BY 1, 2;

items: **Target lag** is the maximum staleness relative to the base tables, not a schedule. `TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM` refreshes only when a dependent Dynamic Table needs it.

**Refresh mode**: `INCREMENTAL` processes only changes; `FULL` recomputes; `AUTO` lets Snowflake choose at creation. Some constructs (certain non-deterministic functions, some window and join shapes) prevent incremental refresh: check the current documentation and the table's refresh mode after creation.
Shorter lag means more frequent refreshes and more credits. Set lag from the consumer's real requirement.

blocks.text: Rough guide: use Dynamic Tables for declarative SQL transformations with minute-level freshness; streams and tasks when you need procedural control, side effects or custom MERGE semantics; dbt (chapter 31) when you want versioned, tested models, possibly materialized as Dynamic Tables.
27.6 Semi-structured data with VARIANT

`VARIANT` stores JSON, Avro, Parquet or XML values. Snowflake extracts frequently occurring paths into columnar storage internally, so queries on common fields prune and scan almost like regular columns. Access paths with `:` and `.`, cast with `::`, and explode arrays with `LATERAL FLATTEN`.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: querying VARIANT
blocks.text:
SELECT
  e.payload:order_id::NUMBER        AS order_id,
  e.payload:customer.country::STRING AS country,
  i.value:sku::STRING                AS sku,
  i.value:qty::NUMBER                AS qty
FROM raw.events e,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:items) i
WHERE e.payload:type::STRING = 'order_placed';

Keep VARIANT in bronze for schema-on-read flexibility, and extract typed columns in silver. A single VARIANT value has a size limit (check the current documentation), and fields that vary wildly in type across rows lose the columnar optimization.

blocks.title: From files to a fresh gold table
blocks.text: An online shop drops order JSON files into S3 every few seconds and builds the pipeline above. End-to-end freshness is under 20 minutes, and the transformation warehouse only starts when the stream has changes.

blocks.title: Choose an ingestion and transformation path
blocks.text: A logistics company has three feeds: hourly CSV exports from an ERP (5 GB each), a Kafka topic of 3,000 GPS events per second, and Postgres CDC delivered as Parquet files every minute. Choose the loading path for each and the transformation mechanism (stream and task, Dynamic Table, or scheduled dbt) to build a silver shipment table refreshed within 10 minutes.
hints: Which feeds arrive as files, and which as rows?
Where will you deduplicate, and on which key?
What does a 10-minute target lag cost compared with 1 hour?

items: Stages and storage integrations give Snowflake governed access to files; file formats describe parsing.
COPY INTO is idempotent per file name through load metadata; size files around 100-250 MB compressed.
Snowpipe loads files on event notifications; Snowpipe Streaming ingests rows with offset tokens for seconds-level latency.
Streams track changes and advance only on committed consumption; tasks schedule the processing.
Dynamic Tables declare a query and a target lag; refresh can be incremental or full.
VARIANT handles semi-structured data; extract typed columns in silver.

blocks.q: A COPY INTO job is rerun after a partial failure over the same set of staged files. What happens to files already loaded?
options: They are skipped because load metadata records them, unless FORCE = TRUE
The COPY fails because the files exist in load history
They are loaded again, creating duplicates
They are deleted from the stage
blocks.explain: Load metadata makes COPY idempotent per file. FORCE = TRUE bypasses it and is the usual cause of duplicates.

blocks.q: A task consumes a stream inside a MERGE, and the MERGE fails. What happens to the stream offset?
options: It advances only for the rows that succeeded
It advances, so the changes are lost
It does not advance, so the next run sees the same changes
blocks.explain: The offset moves only when a DML statement consuming the stream commits. This gives at-least-once processing, which is why the MERGE should be idempotent.

blocks.q: What does TARGET_LAG = '15 minutes' on a Dynamic Table mean?
options: Snowflake aims to keep its contents no more than 15 minutes behind its base tables
Queries on the table time out after 15 minutes
The table refreshes exactly every 15 minutes
blocks.explain: Target lag is a freshness goal; Snowflake schedules refreshes to meet it, which is not the same as a fixed cron interval.

blocks.q: Which path gives seconds-level latency for rows arriving from Kafka without writing intermediate files?
options: COPY INTO on a one-minute task
blocks.explain: Snowpipe Streaming ingests rows through channels directly into tables. Auto-ingest Snowpipe and COPY both load files and have higher latency.
